prize_parts.citation: For the development of halide perovskites as high-efficiency solar cell absorbers

statement.case_for: Halide perovskites remain, after the full first-round exchange, the candidate where the underlying principle, the quantitative evidence and the independent reproduction are all clearest. A structurally simple ABX3 semiconductor with strong absorption, defect tolerance and long carrier diffusion lengths took solution-processed photovoltaics from a few percent to well above 25 percent certified efficiency in roughly a decade, and the result has been reproduced in laboratories worldwide. The discovery is chemical in the sense that matters: composition, crystal structure and defect chemistry set the device physics. The citation I would write rests on the absorber material and its efficiency, not on deployment, so unresolved module lifetime and lead content do not weaken it. The attribution follows the chain of discovery: Miyasaka made the first perovskite-sensitized cell, and Park and Snaith turned it into the solid-state, high-efficiency thin-film device that established the field. Zou and I reach the same trio independently, from the materials and physics sides respectively, which is the only identical laureate set proposed by two members in round 1.
statement.case_against: Credit is genuinely contested: Gratzel, Kanatzidis and Seok made decisive contributions (the solid-state cell, the lead-iodide solid-state work, and the efficiency records), and any three-person cut will be criticised as arbitrary. Operational stability and lead toxicity are open, and a colleague who wants deployment evidence can fairly call a citation premature. Support is also narrow: two explicit preferences in round 1, against two each for B054 and B069 and no configuration near five, so I cannot claim that perovskites are the committee's centre of gravity. I also accept that the third name is the weakest point of my own configuration.

responses.point: Brzezinski proposes Crews, Deshaies and Handa for targeted protein degradation as a single part spanning heterobifunctional degraders and the cereblon glue mechanism, and himself flags that a broad line of work with eight names and no approved PROTAC is the kind of candidacy he normally treats with caution.
responses.response: I take his own caution seriously, and it is the main reason I have not moved B054 into my preferred slot. The ternary-complex and cereblon-degron mechanism work is strong, and I accept it is a new principle rather than a technique. But merging the PROTAC concept (Crews, Deshaies) with the glue mechanism (Handa, Ito) into one citation makes it two lineages with different owners, and Ciulli and Sakamoto remain outside the three names in either case. The chair's question about whether an approval should come first is, to me, secondary to whether the committee can name one separable discovery and its owners; on the round-1 files it has not yet agreed on that. I would move to B054 if the committee settles on one branch with a defensible trio. I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Chabes pairs base editing (Liu alone) with heterobifunctional degraders (Crews, Deshaies) as a coherent prize on chemical control of the genome and the proteome, arguing this draws on the broadest opening support.
responses.response: The pairing is the most carefully argued two-part proposal in the file, and Chabes is candid about its costs. My difficulty is that broad ranking is not the same as a shared unit: a prize on chemical control of genome and proteome is a theme assembled after the fact, whereas each part rests on a different principle and a different contested credit (Komor and Gaudelli, Kondo and Nishida, Handa, Ciulli). Chabes himself concedes that naming Komor and Gaudelli would leave no room for the second part. I would also not treat the 2020 CRISPR prize as disposing of base editing, since it is a chemical conversion on a base rather than a cut, but I share Somfai's question about how much of the chemistry is new beyond known deaminase reactions. This is why I keep B069 as an alternative and have added it in place of B059.

responses.point: Zou ranks perovskites first with the same Miyasaka, Snaith and Park trio and worries that stability and lead toxicity may make colleagues prefer to wait.
responses.response: We agree on the trio and on the open items. After reading the files I take her point that Gratzel's solid-state work is the strongest challenge to the Park name, and I do not think either of us has shown why Park should rank above Gratzel beyond the first efficient solid-state device in 2012 and the priority of publication. I still hold to Park because the decisive step was the move from liquid-electrolyte dye-sensitised cells to stable thin-film solid-state absorbers, which the Park and Snaith groups delivered, and I would leave Gratzel, Kanatzidis and Seok outside only with an explicit statement that this is a three-person limit and not a judgement on their contributions. On stability, I would not accept an argument that it makes the discovery premature, because it concerns the device, not the absorber principle.

responses.point: Somfai pairs Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling (Buchwald, Hartwig) with base editing (Liu), noting that only he ranked B065, that it follows the 2010 cross-coupling prize, and that the two parts are unrelated.
responses.response: I appreciate his straightforward statement that the pairing has a weak unifying citation, and that the committee has not tested B065. C-N coupling is a clean, mechanistically transparent and mature method, and his argument that it complements the 2010 prize rather than duplicates it is reasonable. But with a single supporter and a Kosugi priority question still unresolved, I cannot see it reaching five votes, and a two-part prize of unrelated methods does not give a stronger citation than a single coherent achievement. I would rather the committee compare it with the broader candidates on the final ballot than treat it as a partner for B069 simply to fill a second part.

uncertainties: Whether Gratzel, Kanatzidis or Seok has a stronger claim than Park to the third place beside Miyasaka and Snaith, since the priority record of the 2009-2012 papers is from memory and not verified in the files I may read.
Whether stability and lead toxicity make a perovskite citation premature for enough colleagues to prevent five votes.
Whether the committee can define a single separable discovery in B054 and agree on its laureates, in which case it may become the stronger candidate.
Whether base editing is distinct enough from the 2020 CRISPR prize and from known deaminase chemistry to stand alone.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal need is apparent for any shortlisted candidate: none is linked to Lund University or to my own nanowire, thermoelectric or molecular-motor work. Fellow Lund members Somfai and Sparr are colleagues, which is not a recusal issue. No change from round 1.
